chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Safwan ibn Yahya from 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Zurarah who said:

I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Allah made its sanctuary forbidden, continuously and perpetually, that its plain should not be trodden upon and its trees should not be cut down, except the Idhkhir tree, or its birds should not be hunted. And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) made Medina, what is between its two lava flows, forbidden for its game, and He made what is around it forbidden, continuously and perpetually, that its plain should not be trodden upon and its trees should not be cut down, except the two branches of the fodder of the beast of burden.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And the Muhrim (one in minor pilgrimage state) if he kills game in the Sanctuary, upon him is its ransom, and likewise if he kills it in what is between Medina and the Sanctuary. And this we have explained in what preceded. Then he said (may Allah have mercy on him): And the Muhrim if he puts out the eye of the game or breaks its horn, he should give charity. And this also has preceded its mention. Then he said (may Allah have mercy on him): And if the Muhrim commands his slave to hunt while he (the slave) is Muhrim, and he kills it, then upon the master is the ransom.

key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: the one in Ihram (state of consecration)
key_terms.عُودَيْ مَحَالَةِ النَّاضِحِ: the two branches of the fodder of the beast of burden
key_terms.فَقَأَ عَيْنَ الصَّيْدِ: put out the eye of the game

ai.seo_question: What are the rules of hunting and compensation in Mecca and Medina according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) delineates the specific boundaries of the Haramain, distinguishing between the sanctity of Mecca and the broader protection of Medina, while establishing the principle of fidyah for hunting violations. Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this by clarifying that the ruling applies equally to those in Ihram and those outside it, and extends liability to the master if a slave hunts by command, reflecting the juristic emphasis on agency and compensation in Shia fiqh. The hadith underscores the ecological and spiritual sanctity of these regions, linking physical preservation of nature to ritual purity.
